prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned prose that builds an encyclopedic inner cosmos from memory, the body and dream, and for a sustained imaginative project in Romanian fiction and poetry.

statement.case_for: On the common criteria, Cărtărescu is my strongest candidate. His voice is distinctive: public knowledge of Blinding and Solenoid points to long architectural structures, recurring image systems and sustained linguistic intensity that make memory, the body and metaphysical speculation into one imaginative enterprise. The formal achievement is the scale and patterning of the prose, not the subject matter alone. The intellectual depth lies in how the work treats consciousness and inherited literary tradition across genres. The poetry background and the late major novels suggest a consolidated oeuvre whose project has already taken shape. A single-writer citation fits cleanly: it can name the prose cosmos without resting on national symbolism or fame. This is a judgment from general public knowledge, not from independently verified reading.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the case rests on Romanian prose whose density, rhythm and patterning I can only judge indirectly through translation. His longest books may divide readers between sustained vision and excess or repetition, and I cannot independently confirm which reading is right. Coverage of the poetry and early work in translation is also thinner than for the major novels. The committee should therefore keep the citation anchored in the prose it can actually assess, and should not assume the poetry carries equal weight.

responses.point: Olsson sees a unified body of work across genres, with a lineage from modernist and Romantic traditions, and also flags that the long, digressive structures may divide readers between quality and excess.
responses.response: I agree that the question of vision versus excess is the central test of the case, and I do not think it can be settled by asserting the work's scale. I would qualify the poetry-to-prose unity argument. Given thin translation coverage of the poetry, I would anchor the citation on the novels, with the poetry as an origin of the vision rather than an independently assessed pillar. That keeps the citation within what we can honestly weigh.

responses.point: Mattson rates Can Xue second for an uncompromising, consistent narrative method, and asks whether that uniformity reads as rigor or as repetition. She also notes that only part of the output is translated.
responses.response: I share that uncertainty, and it is why I keep Can Xue as a serious alternative rather than my first choice. Her radicalism and consistency are real merits. But the same open question of rigor versus repetition, combined with partial translation of a very large output, makes sustained quality harder for me to establish than for Cărtărescu, whose major novels show a project that expands and deepens. I would not weigh that difference lightly, but I also would not call it decisive. My ranking reflects a closer judgment than a gap in quality.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Pierre Michon third for compressed, sculpted French prose of great concentration, while raising doubts about whether Carson's hybrid and visual forms fit the will's conventional notion of the literary work.
responses.response: I take the Carson concern seriously. Some of her books depend on physical or visual design, so the citation should rest on her written poetry and essays, not on object-books or translation. I still see her formal reinvention and unmistakable voice as stronger than the objection, which is why I keep her second. On Michon, I admire the language-level achievement, but a compact oeuvre makes significance across a body of work harder to argue than for a writer with a broader, still-developing project. That is a question of breadth, not of depth.

responses.point: Sward ranks Yoko Tawada second, arguing that bilingual writing in Japanese and German makes linguistic estrangement a formal principle across several genres, and that her two-language practice is part of the achievement.
responses.response: I agree that Tawada's two-language practice is an achievement and not an attribution problem. My hesitation is evidentiary. A fair assessment requires competence in both the Japanese and the German work, and wordplay is the element that translation damages most. I ranked her fifth because I cannot confirm how representative the translated corpus is. I would want colleagues who read either language to say specifically which works carry the case before I moved her up.

responses.point: Palm ranks Anne Carson second, and notes that the citation scope would need to define how genre-crossing work fits Nobel's will and an ideal direction.
responses.response: I agree that scope is the real weakness of the Carson case, and I stated it in my own opening. If the committee preferred her, the citation would need to name formal reinvention at the meeting of poetry, essay and classical material, and would need to separate her original work from her scholarship and translation. A citation defined that tightly is possible but less self-evident than one for Cărtărescu, whose scope is easier to state.

uncertainties: How well the density and musicality of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose carries in translation, and whether the longest novels sustain their quality or lapse into excess, cannot be settled from my public knowledge.
Translation coverage of his poetry and early work is partial, so how much the poetry should figure in a citation is unresolved.
For Can Xue, Adonis and Tawada, assessment depends on how representative the translated corpus is of the original-language work.
I have not independently verified any source or read the works for this exercise, and I rely on general public knowledge and colleagues' stated views.
Whether a co-opted member's vote counts in the actual committee is undocumented. My simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-relevant connection to any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile. Documented connections are only to colleagues and family: marriage to Pär Nuder, election to the Academy alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg, and working with chair Anders Olsson. My own non-fiction practice is context, not evidence of preference for any candidate.
